title: FIR Registered Against You? Here Is Exactly What to Do
excerpt: Being named in an FIR is frightening — but there are clear legal steps to protect yourself from day one.
content:
Having a First Information Report (FIR) lodged against you in Pakistan is one of the most stressful legal situations a person can face. The fear of arrest, the uncertainty of the process, and the social stigma can feel overwhelming. But with the right legal steps taken immediately, your rights can be protected.

Step 1: Contact an Advocate Immediately

The single most important thing you can do when you learn an FIR has been lodged against you is to contact an advocate before speaking to anyone else — especially the police. Anything you say without legal representation can and will be used against you. An experienced criminal lawyer will assess the FIR, identify its weaknesses, and advise on the immediate strategy.

Step 2: Apply for Pre-Arrest Bail

Pre-arrest bail (also called protective bail or anticipatory bail) is a court order that prevents your arrest while the case proceeds. It is filed in the Sessions Court or the High Court depending on the nature of the offence. Securing pre-arrest bail should be the very first legal move — it keeps you out of custody and allows you to participate in your own defence from a position of freedom.

Step 3: Understand the FIR and the Offences Cited

Not all FIRs are equal. Many are filed with exaggerated or incorrect sections of the Pakistan Penal Code. Your advocate will analyse exactly which sections have been cited, whether they are bailable or non-bailable, and whether any sections can be challenged or quashed before the High Court.

Step 4: Consider Quashing the FIR

The High Court has the power to quash an FIR that is frivolous, malicious, or does not disclose a cognisable offence. If the FIR against you is based on a false complaint, a quashing petition is often the fastest route to resolution — avoiding a full trial entirely.

title: A Complete Guide to Khula in Pakistan: Process, Timeline & Your Rights
excerpt: Khula is a woman's legal right to divorce in Pakistan. Here is everything you need to know about the process.
imageAlt: Family law consultation representing divorce proceedings
content:
Khula is the right granted to a Muslim wife to seek dissolution of her marriage through the courts when the marriage has broken down irretrievably. Unlike talaq (which is the husband's prerogative), khula is initiated by the wife through the Family Court. It is a well-established legal right under Pakistani family law.

Who Can Apply for Khula?

Any Muslim wife who finds it impossible to continue living with her husband — for any reason she considers valid — has the right to seek khula. The courts have consistently held that a wife does not need to prove specific misconduct by the husband; her genuine desire for dissolution is sufficient grounds.

The Khula Process Step by Step

The wife files a suit for dissolution of marriage in the Family Court of the area where she resides or where the marriage took place. The court issues summons to the husband. An Arbitration Council is formed to attempt reconciliation. If reconciliation fails (or the husband does not appear), the court proceeds to dissolve the marriage. The wife is typically required to return the mehr (dower) received at marriage, though courts may reduce this amount.

Timeline: How Long Does Khula Take?

An uncontested khula where the husband cooperates or does not appear can be concluded in 3 to 4 months. A contested khula where the husband opposes the suit may take 6 to 12 months or longer. In urgent circumstances involving abuse or abandonment, courts can expedite proceedings.

Your Rights After Khula

After khula is granted, the wife is entitled to observe iddat (a waiting period of three menstrual cycles). During iddat, the husband is responsible for her accommodation and maintenance. Children's custody and maintenance are separate matters determined by the court in the children's best interest.

title: Child Custody Laws in Pakistan: What Every Parent Must Know
excerpt: Custody disputes are emotionally painful. Understanding the law clearly helps parents make the best decisions for their children.
imageAlt: Parent and child representing custody law
content:
Child custody disputes are among the most emotionally charged legal matters handled by the courts. In Pakistan, custody law is primarily governed by the Guardians and Wards Act 1890 and Islamic principles of hizanat (physical custody). Understanding how courts approach these cases is essential for any parent involved in a separation or divorce.

The Paramount Principle: Best Interest of the Child

Pakistani courts apply one overriding principle in all custody matters: what is in the best interest of the child? All other considerations — the preferences of either parent, financial status, or religious arguments — are secondary to this central question.

Mother's Right of Hizanat

Under Islamic law as applied in Pakistani courts, the mother has the right of physical custody (hizanat) of children up to age 7 for boys and until puberty for girls. After these ages, the child's own wishes are given significant weight. The mother may lose this right if she remarries a person unrelated to the child, or if she is found to be unfit.

Father's Right of Guardianship

Even when physical custody rests with the mother, the father retains legal guardianship — including responsibility for the child's education, healthcare, and financial maintenance. The father also has visitation rights, which the court will define if the parties cannot agree.

What If the Other Parent Refuses Visitation?

Refusing a court-ordered visitation arrangement is contempt of court and can result in serious legal consequences. If the other parent is withholding your child in violation of a court order, an application can be filed immediately to enforce the order.

title: How to Legally Verify Property Before Buying in Islamabad
excerpt: Property fraud is common in Pakistan. A proper legal check before purchase can save you everything.
imageAlt: Property keys and documents on a desk
content:
Property fraud is one of the most financially devastating crimes in Pakistan. Fraudulent sellers, duplicate registrations, forged title deeds, and plots sold to multiple buyers simultaneously have ruined families who invested their life savings without proper legal verification. Before signing any property agreement in Islamabad, a thorough legal check is not optional — it is essential.

Verify the Title Chain

The seller must be able to produce the original title deed and show an unbroken chain of ownership going back at least two transfers. Each transfer must be supported by registered sale deeds or allotment letters from the relevant authority (CDA, DHA, PHATA, etc.). Any gap in the chain is a major red flag.

Check for Mortgages, Encumbrances & Court Orders

A property can be legally sold even when it is mortgaged to a bank or subject to a court injunction — if the buyer is not warned. We search the relevant court records and land registries to confirm the property is free of all encumbrances before you commit to purchase.

Verify with the Relevant Authority

For CDA sectors, verification can be obtained from CDA directly. For DHA properties, DHA Islamabad records must be checked. For private housing schemes, the legal status of the scheme itself must be verified — many schemes in Islamabad's periphery are unapproved and carry serious title risk.

Confirm Physical Possession

Title verification alone is not enough. Physical possession must be confirmed. We advise clients to visit the property in person, check for any occupants or encroachers, and confirm the plot boundaries match the documents.

Get a Legal Opinion Before You Pay

A formal legal opinion from an advocate, obtained before you pay any token money or sign any agreement, is the most valuable investment you can make in a property transaction. We provide written property due diligence opinions for buyers across Islamabad. Contact us on 0300-5421753.

title: Understanding Bail in Pakistan: Types, Process & How to Get It
excerpt: Bail is a fundamental right in many cases. Understanding the process ensures you or your loved one is not held unnecessarily.
imageAlt: Justice scales representing bail application process
content:
In Pakistan's criminal justice system, bail is the mechanism by which an accused person is released from custody pending the conclusion of their case. Understanding the types of bail, which court to approach, and what arguments succeed is essential knowledge for anyone facing criminal proceedings.

Types of Bail in Pakistan

Pre-arrest bail (protective bail) — obtained before arrest, from the Sessions Court or High Court. Post-arrest bail — applied for after the accused is in custody. Bail before arrest is preferable as it prevents the trauma and risks of detention. Both are governed by Section 496–502 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).

Bailable vs Non-Bailable Offences

In bailable offences (listed in the Second Schedule of the CrPC), bail is a right and must be granted by the police or court. In non-bailable offences, bail is a discretionary concession. For non-bailable offences, the advocate must present compelling arguments — typically that the accused is not a flight risk, the evidence is weak, or exceptional circumstances exist.

Which Court to Approach

For minor offences, bail can be granted by the Judicial Magistrate. For more serious offences (sessions-triable matters), the Sessions Court has jurisdiction. For heinous offences or when lower courts have refused bail, the High Court is the appropriate forum. Rana Muhammad Zahid Muneer regularly argues bail applications before all three tiers.

How Long Does a Bail Application Take?

An urgent pre-arrest bail application can be heard the same day or next day in most cases. Post-arrest bail applications are typically fixed within 3 to 7 days. Where there is genuine urgency, courts can hear matters on an emergency basis.

title: When and How to File a Writ Petition in the Islamabad High Court
excerpt: A writ petition is a powerful constitutional remedy. Knowing when to use it can transform your legal position.
imageAlt: Constitution and legal books representing constitutional law
content:
A writ petition is a direct application to the High Court invoking its constitutional jurisdiction under Article 199 of the Constitution of Pakistan. It is one of the most powerful legal remedies available — cutting through lower court procedures to place your matter directly before the High Court.

What Is a Writ Petition?

A writ petition asks the High Court to issue one of several constitutional orders: Mandamus (directing a public authority to perform a duty), Certiorari (quashing an illegal order), Prohibition (preventing a lower tribunal from exceeding jurisdiction), Quo Warranto (challenging a person's right to hold public office), or Habeas Corpus (securing release of a person illegally detained).

When Should You File a Writ Petition?

Common situations where a writ petition is the right remedy include: a government department refusing to perform its legal duty; an illegal order issued by a public authority; illegal detention or denial of fundamental rights; service disputes where a government employee is wrongfully dismissed or denied promotion; and cases where lower courts are acting without jurisdiction.

Who Has Standing?

Any person whose fundamental rights are infringed, or who is adversely affected by an illegal exercise of public authority, has standing to file a writ petition before the Islamabad High Court.

The Process

The petition is filed with a supporting affidavit and legal arguments. The court may issue a notice to the respondents, fix a date for arguments, and if satisfied, issue an interim order staying the impugned action. Final orders can provide complete relief within weeks in urgent matters.

title: How to Recover Money Through Court in Pakistan
excerpt: Someone owes you money and refuses to pay. Here are the legal options available to you in Pakistan.
imageAlt: Legal documents representing civil money recovery
content:
One of the most common civil legal problems faced by individuals and businesses in Pakistan is the non-payment of money owed — whether under a loan, a contract, a business transaction, or a dishonoured cheque. The good news is that Pakistani law provides effective remedies for money recovery.

Step 1: Send a Legal Notice

Before filing suit, your advocate sends a formal legal notice to the debtor giving them a fixed period (typically 15 to 30 days) to pay the outstanding amount. A formal legal notice from an advocate often achieves payment without any court proceedings — particularly where the debtor has no genuine defence and simply hopes you will not pursue the matter formally.

Step 2: File a Civil Suit for Recovery

If the legal notice is ignored, a suit for recovery of money is filed in the Civil Court of competent jurisdiction. The court issues summons to the defendant, who must file a written statement. If the claim is clear and documented, an application for summary judgment can be filed to avoid a full trial.

Cheque Dishonour: Civil and Criminal Remedies

A dishonoured cheque creates both a civil cause of action (recovery suit) and a criminal offence under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code. Filing both simultaneously — a recovery suit in civil court and a criminal complaint before a Magistrate — is often the most effective strategy as it puts significant pressure on the debtor to settle.

Securing Your Claim: Attachment Before Judgment

Where there is risk that the debtor may dispose of assets before the case concludes, we apply for attachment before judgment — a court order that freezes the debtor's assets to protect your eventual decree.

title: The Legal Notice: Why It Matters and How to Use It Effectively
excerpt: A well-drafted legal notice is often the most cost-effective legal tool available — and most people underestimate it.
imageAlt: Legal documents and professional desk representing legal advisory
content:
A legal notice is a formal written communication sent by an advocate on behalf of a client to another party, informing them of a legal claim or grievance and demanding a specific action — payment, compliance, or cessation of harmful conduct — within a defined period.

Why Send a Legal Notice?

In many civil disputes, a formal legal notice from an advocate achieves the desired result — payment, compliance, or an apology — without any court proceedings. The notice signals that the matter is being taken seriously and that litigation is imminent. For many recipients, the cost and inconvenience of a court case is sufficient motivation to resolve the matter promptly.

When Is a Legal Notice Required by Law?

In some cases, sending a legal notice is a legal prerequisite before filing suit. Under the Civil Procedure Code, suits against government departments require a mandatory two-month notice period. For certain contract matters, a notice of breach is required before termination or damages can be claimed.

What Should a Legal Notice Include?

A properly drafted legal notice includes: the full identity of the sender and recipient; a clear statement of the facts giving rise to the claim; the specific legal rights being invoked; the action demanded (payment amount, specific performance, etc.); a clear deadline for compliance; and the consequences of non-compliance (court proceedings, criminal complaint, etc.).

What Happens If the Notice Is Ignored?

Ignoring a legal notice is not a safe strategy — it simply means the next communication will come from a court. Courts also take note of whether notices were sent and ignored when assessing costs and the conduct of parties.

title: A Practical Guide to the Islamabad High Court: Jurisdiction & Procedure
excerpt: Understanding the Islamabad High Court's jurisdiction helps you know when you have a direct route to the highest court.
imageAlt: High Court building representing Islamabad High Court
content:
The Islamabad High Court (IHC) is the superior court for the Islamabad Capital Territory. Established in 2010 under the Islamabad High Court Act, it exercises original, appellate, and constitutional jurisdiction over all courts and tribunals within Islamabad.

Original Jurisdiction

The IHC has original jurisdiction over constitutional petitions under Article 199 of the Constitution. This means parties can approach the IHC directly — without first going to a lower court — when their fundamental rights are violated or a public authority acts illegally.

Appellate Jurisdiction

The IHC hears appeals from all civil and criminal courts in Islamabad, including decisions of the Sessions Court, Additional District Courts, and various tribunals. Appeals from the Sessions Court in criminal matters, and from the Civil Judge in civil matters, lie before the IHC.

Supervisory Jurisdiction

The IHC also has supervisory jurisdiction over all subordinate courts in Islamabad — it can review and revise any order or judgment of a lower court that is illegal, improper, or based on a misreading of the law, even without a formal appeal being filed.

Who Can Appear Before the IHC?

Only enrolled Advocates High Court have the right of audience before the Islamabad High Court. This is an important distinction — matters before the IHC require an advocate with specific High Court enrolment and experience in superior court procedure.
